mind
------------------------------------------
Introduction
Hindu view of life accords great importance to the मिन्द् since both abhyu-daya (worldly prosperity) and niśśreyasa (spiritual progress) depend upon its condition. An impure मिन्द् binds the सोउल् to transmigratory existence whereas a pure मिन्द् leads to मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् (Amṛta-बिन्दु Upaniṣad 2).
While recognising the importance of the मिन्द् as a distinguishing unique feature of human beings, the Hindu scriptures and the various systems of Hindu philosophy have given different views about its content, nature and function. A study of the मिन्द्, therefore, will not only be interesting but also useful in one’s personal life of spiritual evolution.
What the मिन्द् is
The Chāndogya Upaniṣad (6.6.5) declares that the मिन्द् is ‘annamaya,’ made up of the subtle essence of ड़ोओद्. It also asserts that purity of ड़ोओद् conduces to purity of मिन्द् (ibid 7.26.2).
The Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad (

) describes the मिन्द् as having been produced from ईश्वर or हिरण्यगर्भ (Creator). It also declares, though indirectly, that the सोउल् or the Self (ātman) knows the external world through the मिन्द् (vide 1.5.3).
The Sāṅkhya and the योग systems consider the मिन्द् as a product evolved from the insentient प्रकृति, a direct product from अहङ्कार (the ego-principle) and hence made up of the three guṇas—sattva, रजस् and तमस्. It is also, therefore, jaḍa or insentient but can reflect the चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् of the पुरुष or the आत्मन् (the सोउल्).
The न्याय-Vaiśeṣika schools consider the मनस् or the मिन्द् as one of the dravyas (fundamental or basic realities) out of which the world is eventually created. It acts as a link between the सोउल् and the sense-organs by which the external objects are known.
Certain cults of शैविस्म् and Śāktāism (tantras) advocate the theory that मिन्द् is a limitation or a modification of pure चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स्.
As regards the size of the मिन्द्, some systems like न्याय and Vaiśeṣika hold it as aṇu (atomic) while others (Advaita Vedānta) consider it as vibhu (all-pervading).
Importance of the Mind
The ultimate purpose of human life is to attain मोक्ष or लिबेरतिओन् from transmigratory existence. This is possible only when sādhanā or spiritual practice is undertaken as per the dictates of the scriptures. Sādhanā consists mainly in purifying the मिन्द् through proper personal मोरलित्य्, social एथिच्स् and religions observances. When the मिन्द् becomes completely pure, the आत्मन् inside is automatically revealed.
Impurities of the मिन्द् are of three types: basic impurity due to its being a product of the three guṇas (sattva, रजस् and तमस्); impurities carried over from the previous lives, technically called ‘saṁskāras’; impurities due to the sins and evils committed in this life.
The third one can be offset by the performance of prāyaścittas or expiatory rites prescribed in the holy books as also by experiencing the suffering brought about by them. The second has to be counteracted by trying hard to cultivate the opposite, good, tendencies. When these are carried out, along with निदिध्यासन or meditation on oneself as the pure आत्मन् (ultimately one with ब्रह्मन्) or any aspect of God, the rājāsik and the tāmasik contents of the मिन्द् gradually get attenuated and the sāttvik part gets predominance. When this process is completed, realisation can come in a flash.
Mind and the Ātman
Most of the Hindu philosophical systems consider the मिन्द् either as an उपाधि (limiting adjunct) or as a quality of the jīvātman (the individual सोउल्). It is through the मिन्द् that the jīvātman knows the external world or gets internal experiences.
Functions of the Mind
There are several ways of looking at the functions of the मिन्द्. Works on Vedānta generally define the मिन्द् as ‘antaḥkaraṇa’ (the inner organ) and state that it has four aspects: मनस् (general thinking and चोग्नितिओन्); बुद्धि (discriminative faculty); अहङ्कार (ego-sense); चित्त (mind-stuff, responsible for memory).
According to another view it has three qualities or functions or modifications: jñānātmaka (cognitive); āvegātmaka (emotional); prayatnātmaka (volitional).
Cognition, again, can produce either प्रमा (true knowledge) or भ्रम (false knowledge). The latter includes सṁशय or doubt also.
Pramā or true knowledge can be produced by six ways out of which प्रत्यक्ष (direct perception), अनुमान (inference) and āptavākya (verbal testimony of reliable persons) are universally accepted. शब्द or Śruti or Āgama is an extension of the last, as applied to things beyond the ken of the senses.
The emotional functions of the मिन्द् can be listed as follows: sukha (pleasure or happiness), दुःख (pain or unhappiness), icchā (desire) and द्वेष (hatred).
Many other kinds of emotions are also recognised, such as bhaya (fear), hāsya (laughter), vismaya (wonder) and so on.
Vedāntic works often mention three states of चोन्स्चिओउस्नेस्स् with a view to proving that the आत्मन् (the सोउल्) is the pure spirit beyond them. These three states—all of the mind—are जाग्रत् (waking state), स्वप्न (dream state) and सुषुप्ति (deep-sleep state).
Extra-sensory Perceptions
Besides these states of the मिन्द् normally experienced by all, there is another, the extra-ordinary or the extra-sensory perception. Highly evolved spiritual persons have attained these states like clairvoyance, clairaudience and so on, which have been described in the standard treatises of योग like the Yogasūtras of पतञ्जलि (200 B. C.) (vide 3.16-55). However these have been considered as obstacles to the final emancipation since they tempt the sādhaka to misuse them.
Conclusion
The main purpose behind the study of the मिन्द् is to facilitate its ultimate purification leading to the realisation of the आत्मन् or the Self. Though there are differences of opinion regarding its nature, the processes of purification are almost universally accepted.
